set_title: Hypersensitivity types I to IV
stem: A 23-year-old woman has worn latex gloves daily for 2 years as a nursing assistant. Two days after a long shift, she has itchy, red, swollen skin on both hands and wrists that stops sharply at the glove line. She has no wheeze, fever or joint pain.
oneliner: 23F + latex gloves for 2 years + itchy red swollen hands to the glove line 2 days after a shift → ?
ask: Which hypersensitivity mechanism is most likely?

options.B: Type II (antibody to cell or matrix antigen)

whyNot.A: Type I appears **within minutes** of contact; her rash appeared 2 days after the shift
whyNot.B: Type II needs **antibody against a cell or matrix antigen** (hemolysis, cytopenia, one target organ); she has a rash only where the gloves touched
whyNot.C: Type III is **systemic, with fever, joint pain and low complement**; she has none of these
whyNot.E: Direct mast cell activation is **immediate and needs no sensitization**; her rash appeared 2 days after exposure

why: A rash confined to the area of contact that appears 48 to 72 hours later means **sensitized T cells** have been recalled to the skin. Latex can cause both type IV and type I reactions; the timing tells them apart.

set_title: Blisters in an adult or child: where the skin splits and why
stem: A 55-year-old man has had painful erosions in his mouth for 2 months. Flaccid blisters then appeared on his scalp and trunk and break easily. Rubbing normal-looking skin next to a blister makes the top layer slide off.
oneliner: 55M + 2 months of mouth erosions + flaccid scalp and trunk blisters + skin slips off with rubbing → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Bullous pemphigoid gives tense blisters and usually spares the mouth; he has **mouth erosions first, flaccid blisters that break easily and skin that slides off with rubbing**
whyNot.B: Dermatitis herpetiformis gives grouped vesicles on the elbows, knees and buttocks without mouth disease; he has **mouth erosions and flaccid blisters on the scalp and trunk**
whyNot.D: Toxic epidermal necrolysis develops over days after a new drug; his disease evolved over **2 months, starting in the mouth**
whyNot.E: Porphyria cutanea tarda blisters the sun-exposed backs of the hands and spares the mouth; he has **mouth erosions and blisters on the scalp and trunk**

why: Autoantibodies against desmoglein 3 and desmoglein 1 destroy the desmosomes that bind keratinocytes to each other, so cells separate just above the basal layer (suprabasal acantholysis). The roof of the blister is thin, so blisters are flaccid, burst into erosions and the Nikolsky sign is positive. **Painful mouth erosions followed by flaccid blisters that shear with rubbing** is pemphigus vulgaris; biopsy and immunofluorescence show net-like IgG around keratinocytes.

stem: A 46-year-old man started phenytoin 2 weeks ago. He now has fever, a painful dusky red rash with blisters, and erosions in his mouth. The epidermis has slid off over 35% of his body surface.
oneliner: 46M + phenytoin 2 weeks ago + fever + painful dusky blistering rash + mouth erosions + 35% detachment → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Pemphigus vulgaris evolves over months and is not tied to a new drug; his illness began **2 weeks after phenytoin with fever and 35% detachment**
whyNot.B: Bullous pemphigoid gives tense blisters in older adults and usually spares the mouth; he has **fever, mouth erosions and sloughing after a new drug**
whyNot.C: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome splits the superficial epidermis, spares the mouth and affects young children; he is an adult with **mouth erosions and a new drug**
whyNot.D: Dermatitis herpetiformis gives itchy grouped vesicles on the extensor surfaces; he has **painful dusky skin that slides off, with mouth erosions after a new drug**

why: A drug-specific cytotoxic T-cell response kills keratinocytes across the full thickness of the epidermis, so the epidermis detaches from the dermis (positive Nikolsky sign) and the mucosa erodes. stem: A 20-month-old girl has fever and large flaccid blisters over her trunk and abdomen that peel with light pressure. Her mouth is not involved.
oneliner: 20-month-old girl + fever + large flaccid trunk blisters that peel + mouth spared → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Pemphigus vulgaris typically presents in adults with mouth erosions; she is **20 months old and her mouth is not involved**
whyNot.B: Bullous pemphigoid gives tense blisters in older adults; she is a toddler with **fever and flaccid blisters that peel**
whyNot.D: Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis erode the mucosa; her **mouth is not involved**

options.D: A biopsy split in the stratum granulosum
